title: Understand how sustainable farming systems conserve natural resources

lessons.title: Natural resources and why we must look after them
lessons.html:
What are natural resources?

Natural resources are things from nature that farming needs. We did not make them, and many of them are hard to replace.

  • Soil: plants grow in it. Good topsoil takes hundreds of years to form.
  • Water: from rain, rivers, dams and boreholes.
  • Veld and grass: food for cattle, sheep and goats.
  • Plants and trees: they hold the soil and give shade.
  • Animals, birds and insects: bees pollinate crops, and birds eat pests.
  • Air and sunlight: plants need them to grow.

What is sustainable farming?

Sustainable farming means farming in a way that we can keep doing for many years. We use resources today, but we leave them in good condition for our children. A sustainable farm makes money, looks after its people and looks after nature.

How resources get damaged

  • Soil erosion: rain and wind carry away bare soil. You see dongas (deep gullies) on the land.
  • Overgrazing: too many animals in a camp for too long. The good grass dies and bare patches appear.
  • Wasting water: leaking pipes, overflowing troughs, watering in the hot midday sun.
  • Pollution: chemicals, diesel and rubbish getting into soil and water.
  • Cutting trees and burning veld at the wrong time.

When resources are damaged, the farm produces less. Crops grow badly, animals get thin and water runs short in dry years. In South Africa, much of the land is dry and rain is not reliable, so this matters a lot.

The law also protects resources. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 deals with protecting soil, water and veld on farms.

lessons.title: Farming practices that conserve resources
lessons.html:
Looking after the soil

  • Keep the soil covered with plants, crop leftovers or mulch. Covered soil does not wash away.
  • Plough along the contour of a slope, not up and down it.
  • Rotate crops. For example, plant beans after maize. Beans put nitrogen back into the soil.
  • Add compost and manure to feed the soil.
  • Fill small erosion channels early, before they become dongas.

Looking after water

  • Fix leaks and report broken pipes and troughs.
  • Water crops early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
  • Use drip irrigation where possible. It puts water at the roots.
  • Collect rainwater from roofs into tanks.

Looking after the veld

  • Move animals from camp to camp so grass can rest and grow back.
  • Do not keep more animals than the veld can feed.
  • Report bare patches and invasive plants such as wattle and prickly pear.

Looking after plants and animals in nature

  • Do not kill bees, birds or harmless snakes and insects for no reason.
  • Keep strips of natural plants next to rivers and fields.
  • Spray chemicals only as instructed and never near water.

Reducing waste

  • Turn manure and plant waste into compost.
  • Put rubbish in the right place. Never burn plastic.
  • Return empty chemical containers to the chemical store for proper disposal.

Small actions every day add up. When each worker closes a tap, moves animals on time or reports a leak, the whole farm saves resources and money.

Key points

  • Natural resources include soil, water, veld, plants and animals.
  • Sustainable farming lets us keep farming for many years.
  • Cover the soil and work along contours to stop erosion.
  • Save water by fixing leaks and watering at cool times.
  • Rotate camps so the veld can rest.
